title: School Days
description: Ten stories about learning and teaching: a new teacher, a reading project, an adult reading class, online school, a parent-teacher meeting, a scholarship and more.

lessons.title: My First Week as a Teacher
lessons.summary: A new English teacher keeps a diary of her nervous first week and learns to build a routine.
lessons.text:
Sunday, August 27

My name is Anna Price, and tomorrow I start my first job as a teacher. I am newly employed at Hillcrest Middle School, where I will teach English to 3 classes of seventh grade students. I have wanted this job since I was a child, so I should be happy. Instead, I am nervous. All evening I have had a pit in my stomach. People talk about "a pit in your stomach" when they have a heavy, nervous feeling inside, and that is exactly how I feel.

Monday, August 28

This morning, the principal, Mrs. Lopez, came to my room before the first bell. She told me that she had been nervous on her first day too, 25 years earlier. She said that the pit in her stomach had disappeared by lunch. Her words put me at ease. To "put someone at ease" means to help them relax, and she put me at ease with one smile.

My first class did not go perfectly. When a boy dropped his books on the floor on purpose, I didn't know how to react. I reacted too slowly, and some students laughed. However, the rest of the day went better.

Wednesday, August 30

An older teacher, Mr. Brooks, has been very helpful. Yesterday he gave me a helpful piece of advice: build a routine and repeat it every day. He said that students feel safe when they know what will happen next. So now every class has the same routine. First, we read quietly for 10 minutes. Then we talk about the reading, and finally we write.

Friday, September 1

Today the boy who had dropped his books asked me for a book to take home. This time I knew how to react: I smiled and gave him one of my favorites. The routine is working. Even though I am still a little nervous every morning, I feel more confident. By the end of the week, the class had settled into the new routine, and so had I.

I wish someone had told me earlier that every new teacher feels this way. If I had known, I would have slept better on Sunday night. Now that I am employed at a school I love, I have a lot to learn, but I am ready.

Questions:
Where is Anna newly employed?
She is newly employed at Hillcrest Middle School, where she teaches English.
What does "a pit in your stomach" mean?
It means a heavy, nervous feeling inside.
What did Mrs. Lopez tell Anna?
She told Anna that she had been nervous on her first day too.
What helpful advice did Mr. Brooks give her?
He told her to build a routine and repeat it every day.
What is the routine in every class?
First the students read quietly, then they talk about the reading, and finally they write.
How did Anna feel at the end of the week?
She felt more confident, and the class had settled into the new routine.

lessons.title: The Reading Passport
lessons.summary: A school newsletter reports on a year-long project in which students collect a stamp for every book they read.
lessons.text:
In September, every student at Jefferson Middle School received a small blue book called a reading passport. It looks like a real passport, but instead of countries, it collects books. Each time a student finishes a book and talks about it with a teacher, the teacher puts a stamp in the passport. A full page holds 10 stamps.

The inspiration for the project came from the school's reading teacher, Mr. Hart. He found his inspiration on a family trip, when his young daughter got a stamp in her passport at every border. "She loved to flip through the pages and count her stamps," he said. "I thought, why not do the same with books?"

Students can choose almost any book. Some pick adventure stories, others pick funny books about ordinary kids, and a few older students even pick romantic novels. Mr. Hart also made a short list of classic books, which teachers sometimes call "the canon." The canon is a group of old, important books that many people believe everyone should read. "Some students think the canon is boring," Mr. Hart said. "But a book is only boring until you find the right one. Romantic stories, sad stories, ordinary stories: they can all lead a reader to the classics."

Many teachers decided to combine the passport with other subjects. In art class, students drew new covers for their favorite books. In history class, they combined reading with research about the time when each story was written.

By the end of May, teachers had given out more than 4,000 stamps. The record holder is a sixth grade student named Ella Kim, who collected 61 stamps. As the record holder, Ella won a gift card for the local bookstore. "Before this year, I thought reading was boring," she said. "Now I flip through my passport every night to see how far I've come."

The year ended with a big celebration in the gym. Every passport holder with at least 10 stamps was invited. At the celebration, students talked about their favorite books, ate cake and received a new, empty passport for the summer. Mr. Hart said that the project would continue next year. "This year, ordinary kids became real readers," he said. "That is worth a celebration."

Questions:
What is a reading passport?
It is a small book that collects stamps for books instead of countries.
When does a student get a stamp?
A student gets a stamp after finishing a book and talking about it with a teacher.
Where did Mr. Hart find his inspiration?
He found it on a family trip, when his daughter got stamps in her passport.
What is "the canon"?
It is a group of old, important books that many people believe everyone should read.
How did teachers combine the passport with other subjects?
In art class students drew book covers, and in history class they combined reading with research.
Who is the record holder, and what did she win?
Ella Kim is the record holder, and she won a gift card for the bookstore.

lessons.title: The Orange Cake
lessons.summary: A cook who never learned to read well joins an adult reading class and finally reads a recipe by herself.
lessons.text:
Rosa Martinez had worked as a cook for 30 years, but she had never learned to read well. She had left school at 12 to help her family, and since then she had rarely needed to read. At work, she knew every recipe by heart. She knew how much butter went into each dish and how long to cook the rice. Rosa rarely talked about it, and nobody at the restaurant knew.

Then the restaurant got a new owner, who gave every cook a printed list of new recipes. Rosa looked at the paper and felt deeply embarrassed. That evening, she found out about a free reading class for adults at the public library. It took her 2 weeks to be brave enough to go.

The teacher was a retired Army colonel named Walter Hayes. He had taught young soldiers for many years, and now he helped adults learn to read twice a week. On the first night, Rosa told him that she had tried to learn before and had always given up. She said that she was disappointed in herself. The colonel listened carefully. Then he said, "You were a child who had to work. You did nothing wrong, so there is nothing to forgive. But if you are still angry at yourself, you should forgive yourself. Then we can begin."

Rosa was brave. She came to every class, even when she was tired after work. The colonel brought recipes to class because he knew that she loved cooking. One night they read a recipe for an orange cake together, word by word: "Melt the butter in a pan. Mix the melted butter with sugar, eggs, flour and the juice of 2 oranges." Rosa read slowly, but she read every word without a mistake. She was deeply proud of herself, and this time she was not disappointed at all.

After 6 months, Rosa could read a whole recipe without help. One evening, she brought an orange cake to class. She had made it at home from a recipe in a book, and she had read every line herself. The colonel said it was the best cake he had ever eaten. "I can taste the orange juice," he said.

"I wish I had come here 20 years ago," Rosa told him. "If I had been brave earlier, I would have saved myself a lot of worry." The colonel smiled. "You came when you were ready," he said. "That is what matters."

Questions:
Why had Rosa rarely needed to read?
She knew every recipe by heart, so she rarely needed to read at work.
How did Rosa feel when she saw the new recipes?
She felt deeply embarrassed.
Who was her teacher?
Her teacher was a retired Army colonel named Walter Hayes.
What did the colonel tell her about forgiving?
He told her that there was nothing to forgive, but that she should forgive herself.
What did the orange cake recipe say?
It said to melt the butter and mix it with sugar, eggs, flour and orange juice.
What did Rosa wish?
She wished she had come to the class 20 years earlier.

lessons.title: School Through the Sky
lessons.summary: A girl who lives on a remote farm writes to her cousin about taking her classes online through a satellite.
lessons.text:
Hi Megan,

You asked me what it is like to go to school online, so here is my answer.

As you know, our farm is in a remote part of Montana. The nearest school is 70 miles away, so I take all my classes online. Living in such a remote place has some problems. For example, the power lines of the utility company don't reach our house. The utility company says it would cost too much to build them. So we make our own electricity with solar panels on the roof. In winter, when the days are short, we have to be careful with electricity. Dad also bought an automatic machine that starts by itself when the batteries are empty. The automatic machine is loud, but it works.

Our internet comes from a satellite. There is a big dish on the roof that talks to a satellite far above the earth. The only real problem is electrical storms. During an electrical storm in July, lightning hit a tree near the house, and an electrical part in the dish stopped working. I missed 3 days of school until a new part arrived.

Classes are better than you might think. My teachers communicate with us by video, email and chat. My math teacher, Mr. Owens, is great at communicating difficult ideas. Last week he taught us about pi. Pi is about 3.14. It shows how many times longer the distance around a circle is than the distance across it. To show us, he asked us to measure a round plate at home. My plate gave me 3.1, which is very close to pi!

Mr. Owens always asks for our input. At the end of each month, we fill out a short form, and he uses our input to improve his lessons. Because of my input, he now records every lesson, so I can watch it again if the satellite connection drops.

The best part of living here is the night sky. There are no city lights, so you can see thousands of stars with the naked eye. "The naked eye" means just your own eyes, without any special glasses or tools. Last night I saw a satellite with the naked eye. It looked like a small star moving slowly across the sky. Maybe it was the satellite that brings me my classes!

Write back soon!

Love,
Lucy

Questions:
Why does Lucy take her classes online?
She lives in a remote place, and the nearest school is 70 miles away.
Why doesn't the family get electricity from the utility company?
The company's power lines don't reach the house, because building them would cost too much.
What happened during the electrical storm in July?
Lightning hit a tree near the house, and an electrical part in the dish stopped working.
What is pi?
Pi is a number, about 3.14, that we use to measure circles.
How does Mr. Owens use the students' input?
He uses their input to improve his lessons.
What did Lucy see with the naked eye?
She saw a satellite moving slowly across the sky.

lessons.title: Speak of the Devil
lessons.summary: At a parent-teacher meeting, a father and a teacher make a plan to help a tired boy who loves sports.
lessons.text:
On a cold Thursday evening in November, Mark Diaz walked to his son's school for a parent-teacher meeting. There was a chill in the air, and Mark felt another kind of chill inside, because his son's grades had been dropping all fall. Leo was 12, and he loved 2 things: hockey and swimming. He had hockey practice 3 mornings a week and swimming practice 2 evenings a week.

Leo's teacher, Ms. Ross, welcomed Mark into her room and showed him Leo's work. "Leo is a bright boy," she said. "Essentially, he doesn't have a problem with learning. He has a problem with sleep. He often falls asleep in my first class." Mark explained that hockey practice started at 6 in the morning. Ms. Ross nodded. "That explains a lot," she said.

Then she asked whether Leo played video games at night. Mark admitted that Leo often played until 11. "Many families restrict screen time on school nights," Ms. Ross said. "You don't have to stop it completely. You could restrict it to 1 hour after his school work is done."

She also suggested that they alter his sports schedule. "Maybe he could choose either hockey or swimming this winter, not both," she said. "You can always alter the plan in the spring." She added that the school offered free counseling for students who felt stressed. "Our counseling service helps students plan their time," she said.

Just then, the door opened, and Leo walked in. He had been waiting in the hall. "Well, speak of the devil," Ms. Ross said with a smile. Leo looked confused, so she explained. "People say 'speak of the devil' when the person they are talking about suddenly appears. It's a friendly thing to say. It doesn't mean you are a devil!"

The 3 of them talked together for 20 minutes. Leo agreed to restrict his games to 1 hour on school nights. He chose swimming for the winter. Swimming practice was in the evening, so he could sleep longer in the morning. He also agreed to try one counseling session. "So essentially, I need more sleep and less screen time," he said.

At the door, Leo said, "Bye, Ms. Ross. Thank you." "Bye, Leo. Bye, Mr. Diaz," she answered. On the walk home, Mark didn't notice the chill in the air at all. By January, Leo was sleeping much better, and his grades had improved.

Questions:
Why were Mark and Ms. Ross worried about Leo?
Leo's grades had been dropping, and he often fell asleep in his first class.
What did Ms. Ross say was essentially Leo's problem?
She said that, essentially, Leo had a problem with sleep.
How did Ms. Ross suggest they restrict screen time?
She suggested they restrict it to 1 hour after his school work.
Why did Leo choose swimming for the winter?
He chose swimming because its practice was in the evening, so he could sleep longer.
What does "speak of the devil" mean?
People say it when the person they are talking about suddenly appears.

lessons.title: The Letter from the Dean
lessons.summary: A high school student tells how she took an entrance exam, waited for months and won a college scholarship.
lessons.text:
My name is Grace Bell. In my last year of high school, I knew that my future was at stake. When something is "at stake," you can win it or lose it, depending on what happens. My parents could not pay for college, so without a scholarship, I would have to work for a few years before I could study.

Every year, Lakewood University offered one full scholarship to a student who wanted to work in child welfare. Child welfare is the work of keeping children safe and healthy, and it has been my dream since I first volunteered at a children's center. To apply, I had to pass an entrance exam, write an essay and have an interview.

I studied for the entrance exam for 3 months. The night before the exam, I could hardly sleep. The entrance exam was long and difficult, but when I walked out, I felt that I had done well. A month later, I sent an inquiry to the university to ask when the results would come. Their answer was polite. They wrote that they had received many inquiries and that every student would hear from them by April 1.

Waiting was the hardest part. I felt as if my fate were in the hands of strangers. My grandmother disagreed. She told me that nobody's fate was decided by one letter. She said that I had already worked hard, and that hard work was never wasted, even when the result was not what you wanted.

On March 28, a letter arrived. It was from the dean of the university. "On behalf of Lakewood University, I am pleased to tell you that you have won this year's scholarship," it said. The dean wrote that my essay about child welfare had impressed everyone. That night I wrote back to her on behalf of my whole family to thank her.

The scholarship pays for 4 years of study. In my first year, I will take classes in the humanities, such as history, literature and languages. The dean explained that the humanities teach us how people think and live, and that this is the base of all welfare work.

At first, the prospect of moving to a new city made me nervous. Now the prospect excites me. My future is no longer at stake. It is in my own hands.

Questions:
What does it mean when something is "at stake"?
It means that you can win it or lose it, depending on what happens.
What is child welfare?
It is the work of keeping children safe and healthy.
What did Grace have to do to apply?
She had to pass an entrance exam, write an essay and have an interview.
What did the university answer to her inquiry?
They wrote that they had received many inquiries and that every student would hear from them by April 1.
What did the letter from the dean say?
It said that, on behalf of the university, she had won the scholarship.
Why will she take classes in the humanities?
The dean explained that the humanities teach us how people think and live.

lessons.title: The Robot Club
lessons.summary: A school robot club builds a small robot that finds its way through a set of walls and enters a city fair.
lessons.text:
Every Tuesday after school, 8 students met in the science lab for the robot club. Their teacher, Mr. Chen, had a simple goal. He wanted them to build a small robot that could find its way through a maze, a set of walls with only one way out.

"How does a robot know where the walls are?" Mr. Chen asked. A girl named Maya said that it needed sensors. "Exactly," he said. "Sensors detect things around the robot. Our robot will have 2 sensors. One will detect walls in front of it, and the other will detect walls on its right."

In the program, the students used a variable called "distance." Mr. Chen explained that a variable is like a box with a name. The number inside the box can change. When the robot moves closer to a wall, the number in the variable gets smaller. When the variable is less than 4 inches, the robot turns.

Mr. Chen also told them that scientists sometimes study how rats learn by putting them in a maze. "A rat remembers which turns lead to food," he said. "Our robot will be a little like a rat. It will remember its turns." The students liked this idea, so they named their robot Rat.

Maya asked whether they could build an android one day. Mr. Chen explained that an android is a robot that looks and moves like a human. "Building an android takes a team of specialists and many years of work," he said. "But every android started with a simple robot like ours."

In March, a specialist from a local tech company visited the club. She was a specialist in robot sensors, and she taught the students to be strategic. "Being strategic means making a plan before you act," she said. So the students made a strategic plan and tested one part at a time.

In May, the club entered the city's Young Innovation Fair. The judges were looking for innovation, which means a new idea or a new way of doing something. At first, Rat got stuck in a corner twice. However, the students changed one number in the program, and on the third try, Rat emerged from the maze in 40 seconds. The club won a prize for innovation, and Mr. Chen said he had never been prouder.

Questions:
What did Mr. Chen want the students to build?
He wanted them to build a robot that could find its way through a maze.
What do the robot's sensors detect?
They detect walls in front of the robot and on its right.
What is a variable, according to Mr. Chen?
A variable is like a box with a name, and the number inside it can change.
Why did the students name their robot Rat?
They named it Rat because a rat remembers its turns in a maze, and their robot did too.
What is an android?
An android is a robot that looks and moves like a human.
What happened at the Young Innovation Fair?
Rat emerged from the maze in 40 seconds, and the club won a prize for innovation.

lessons.title: A Garden Behind the School
lessons.summary: A science teacher and her class turn an empty lot full of trash into a green outdoor classroom.
lessons.text:
For years, there was an empty lot behind Lincoln Elementary School. People dumped old tires, broken chairs and bags of trash there, and nobody liked to walk past it. One spring, a science teacher, Ms. Carter, decided to turn the lot into a garden. She wanted to foster a love of nature in her students. To foster something means to help it grow slowly, the way you help a young plant grow.

First, the city helped them remove the trash. A truck took everything to the city dump. "The dump is where a town's trash ends up," Ms. Carter told the class. "When people say a place 'looks like a dump,' they mean it is dirty and messy. Our lot looks like a dump now, but it won't for long."

Then the students went to work. They swept the old stone path, and they swept the dead leaves into big piles. They planted grass seed in the dry ground and watered it every afternoon. After 2 weeks, the first thin green grass came up.

A young activist named Zoe Park came to speak to the class. She was only 16, but she had already started a group that planted trees in the city. "You don't have to be an adult to be an activist," she said. "An activist is anyone who works hard for a change that they believe in." After her visit, several students said they wanted to be activists too.

Next, the class built a small wooden shelter at the end of the garden. It had a roof and 2 benches, so classes could meet outside even when it rained. On hot days, the shelter also gave shade.

Ms. Carter used the garden for many lessons. She taught the students to tell trees apart by their leaves. Each student found a leaf, pressed it in a heavy book and drew it in a notebook. In the summer evenings, crickets sang in the tall grass. The students learned that male crickets make the sound by rubbing their wings together.

By June, the old lot was green and full of life. Nobody dumped trash there anymore. Ms. Carter felt that the garden had fostered something important: her students now cared about the place where they lived.

Questions:
What did people dump in the empty lot?
They dumped old tires, broken chairs and bags of trash.
What does it mean to foster something?
It means to help it grow slowly, the way you help a young plant grow.
What did the students sweep?
They swept the old stone path and the dead leaves.
What did Zoe Park say an activist is?
She said an activist is anyone who works hard for a change that they believe in.
Why did the class build a shelter?
They built it so that classes could meet outside even when it rained.
How do crickets make their sound?
Male crickets make the sound by rubbing their wings together.

lessons.title: A Bench for Mrs. Grant
lessons.summary: In a newspaper column, a former student explains why her old teacher deserves the town's new memorial.
lessons.text:
Last Saturday, our town opened a small memorial in the park next to Hill Street School. It is a wooden bench with a stone beside it, and on the stone is the name of Mrs. Helen Grant, who taught at the school for 41 years. I was one of her students, and I would like to explain why she deserves a memorial.

Many people say that teaching is a noble job. Mrs. Grant never used big words like that, but she lived them. A noble job is one that serves other people more than yourself, and she did exactly that every day.

First, she believed in liberty in the classroom, as long as it came with responsibility. We had the liberty to choose our own books, to sit where we liked and to ask any question. In return, we had to finish what we started.

She also believed that children could learn to govern themselves. Every fall, our class wrote its own rules and elected a class council. The council governed small things, such as the order of the lunch line and the use of the class library. Mrs. Grant told us that a class that governs itself learns how a town or a country is governed.

Fair representation mattered to her, too. Every group in the class had representation on the council: the quiet kids, the loud kids and the new kids. Some teachers favored their best students. Mrs. Grant never favored anyone, and because of that, everyone trusted her.

Her greatest venture began in 1985. Every summer, she took a cart full of books to the town's parks, so that children could read even when the school was closed. The venture started with 30 books. By the time she retired, it had more than 2,000.

For Mrs. Grant, reading was almost a spiritual activity. She used to say that a good book feeds the spirit the way bread feeds the body. You did not have to be religious to understand her. She meant that books help us find meaning and hope. That spiritual side of reading is what she wanted to give every child.

The memorial is simple, which I think she would have liked. If you pass by, sit on the bench and read for a few minutes. That is the kind of memorial she would have wanted.

Questions:
What is the memorial?
It is a wooden bench in the park with a stone that has Mrs. Grant's name on it.
What is a noble job, according to the writer?
It is a job that serves other people more than yourself.
What liberty did the students have?
They had the liberty to choose their own books, to sit where they liked and to ask any question.
What did the class council govern?
It governed small things, such as the lunch line and the class library.
What was Mrs. Grant's greatest venture?
Every summer, she took a cart full of books to the town's parks.
Why was reading a spiritual activity for her?
She believed that books help us find meaning and hope.

lessons.title: A Class Trip to Washington
lessons.summary: A teacher writes to parents from a class trip, after a delayed flight and a busy first day in the capital.
lessons.text:
Dear parents,

I am writing from our hotel in Washington to tell you that all 12 students are safe, happy and very tired. Here is a short report of our first 2 days.

Our flight on Monday was delayed by 3 hours because of a storm. The students were patient, even though the airport was crowded and noisy. After an hour, a rep from the airline came to our gate and explained the situation. The airline rep was very efficient. Within 20 minutes, she had found seats for all of us on a later flight and given each student a meal card. Because there were not enough normal seats left, the airline put 4 of our students in premium seats at the front of the plane. They told me that the premium seats had big chairs and free snacks, and that it was the best part of the trip so far.

We arrived at the hotel at midnight. I had planned to shave early the next morning, but the morning was so busy that I did not have time to shave until the evening. When you see the photos from Tuesday, you will know why I look so tired!

On Tuesday we visited 2 museums and walked past the White House. In spring, Washington is full of tourists, and the lines can be very long. Our guide had an efficient plan: we visited the busiest museum first, before most of the other tourists arrived. Thanks to her plan, we saw everything without waiting for long.

In the afternoon, we met 2 police officers near the museum, or "cops," as the students called them. The cops were happy to answer questions about their work. One of them said that they helped hundreds of tourists every day, mostly with directions. Another said that the most important thing in his job was to stay calm. The students asked so many questions that the cops laughed and said they should all become police officers one day.

Tomorrow we will visit a library and a famous memorial, and on Friday we will fly home on the same airline. I will send another message when we land. Thank you for trusting me with your children.

Best wishes,
Paul Novak

Questions:
Why was the flight delayed?
It was delayed by 3 hours because of a storm.
How did the airline rep help the group?
She found seats for everyone on a later flight and gave each student a meal card.
Why did 4 students sit in premium seats?
There were not enough normal seats left, so the airline put them in premium seats.
Why didn't Mr. Novak shave in the morning?
The morning was so busy that he did not have time to shave until the evening.
What was the guide's efficient plan?
She took the group to the busiest museum first, before most of the other tourists arrived.
What did the cops say about their work?
They said they helped hundreds of tourists every day, mostly with directions.
